title: OOP
objectives: Explain the four pillars with examples

sections.markdown: OOP organizes software as objects — bundles of data and behavior — interacting through well-defined interfaces. Dominant in Java, Kotlin, C# and Dart.

A **car**: you use the wheel and pedals (public interface) without knowing the engine internals (encapsulation). A sports car and a truck are both Vehicles (inheritance) and both drive() differently (polymorphism).
Overusing inheritance. Deep hierarchies are fragile (you wanted a banana but inherited the whole jungle). Prefer **composition over inheritance**.
'Program to an interface, not an implementation.' Depend on abstractions so you can swap a SQL repository for an API one without touching callers.

flashcards.back: Overloading = same name, different params, resolved at compile time. Overriding = subclass redefines a method, resolved at runtime.
Composition (has-a) is more flexible and less fragile than deep inheritance (is-a). Prefer composition.

quiz.q: Hiding internal state behind methods is…
quiz.explain: Encapsulation controls access to an object's internal state.
Overriding is resolved at runtime via dynamic dispatch; overloading is compile-time.
Composition avoids fragile deep hierarchies and is easier to change.

challenges.text: Model a Shape hierarchy with area() and compute total area polymorphically.
Design a payment system with a PaymentMethod interface (Card, UPI, Wallet).
Refactor a deep inheritance tree into composition with injected behaviors.
Build a plugin system where new types register at runtime via a common interface.

interviewQuestions: Explain the four pillars with examples.
Composition vs inheritance — why prefer composition?
Overloading vs overriding? Which is runtime polymorphism?
Abstract class vs interface — when use which?
What does 'program to an interface' mean?
